Debt Dynamics: Policy Implications External Debt, External Shocks, and Vulnerability in LMICs Low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) are facing historically high global uncertainty at a time when external debt stocks have reached historic highs, debt service pressures remain elevated, fiscal space is limited in many countries, and global bond yields continue to rise, tightening financial conditions. This combination matters because external shocks can be more difficult to absorb when governments already face substantial financing needs and limited room to respond. The key vulnerability therefore lies not in exposure to global shocks alone but in how those shocks interact with already-high debt burdens. Adverse

developments in trade, commodity markets, growth, exchange rates, and tighter global financing conditions all have the potential to weaken external and fiscal positions, and high debt levels can amplify their economic and development consequences and impair the effectiveness of policy responses. International Debt Report 2025 documented the scale of external debt burdens and their links to economic growth and vulnerability (World Bank 2025). Building on that assessment, this year’s report focuses on the interactions between external shocks and external debt burdens, and how debt might amplify vulnerabilities when global conditions deteriorate. This chapter examines the channels through which these interactions operate across LMICs. The chapter

further discusses how rising debt service burdens, elevated financing needs, and changing financing patterns are constraining fiscal space and intensifying debt and rollover risks, as well as the policy priorities for strengthening resilience. Finally, food and nutrition security provides a concrete example of these interactions, illustrating how debt burdens may be closely associated with a decline in the affordability of a healthy diet during periods of global stress. Global uncertainty rose sharply in 2025 (figure 2.1) and remained elevated into 2026. The World Uncertainty Index measures broad uncertainty and rose more than fivefold between the third quarter of 2024 and the third quarter of 2025, nearly twice its COVID-19 peak. The Global Economic Policy Uncertainty Index
showed a similar pattern, rising sharply in early 2025 and remaining elevated into 2026 (Ahir et al. 2022; Davis 2016).1

Elevated uncertainty matters because economies remain closely connected to international markets. Yet countries differ in the nature and degree of their external exposure, which shapes how global external shocks affect them. Trade provides an important example. As figure 2.2 shows, global imports and exports of goods and services increased from below 25 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in the early 2000s, were halted by the 2008 global financial crisis, and subsequently rebounded and have fluctuated around 30 percent. Exposure, however, varies significantly across income groups. In 2025, imports accounted for about 34 percent of GDP in low-income economies, compared with exports of about 24 percent; trade flows were much more balanced in high-income economies.

The next section discusses these transmission channels in greater detail, including the roles of trade and financial exposure, exchange rates, inflation, and policy buffers, and how external debt can amplify vulnerabilities when shocks occur.

2. DEBT DyNAmIcs: POLIcy ImPLIcATIONs 53 Transmission of External Shocks External shocks are transmitted to LMICs differently, depending on their structural features. Economies that rely heavily on imports of goods and services for domestic activity are vulnerable to sudden changes in the external environment, such as production shortfalls in major supplier countries, export restrictions, or supply chain disruptions; in contrast, export-oriented economies are more vulnerable to shifts in demand among their trading partners. External shocks also tend to spill more forcefully into LMICs with open financial markets, partly reflecting rapid capital flow movements. In addition, the types of policy frameworks in LMICs are important for the transmission of external shocks. For

example, in economies with flexible exchange rate regimes, the effects of external shocks are partly absorbed through currency movements. In economies with fixed exchange rate regimes, pressure on the exchange rate can be cushioned by using foreign reserves. As discussed later in this chapter, damage from external shocks that LMICs can absorb and the speed of subsequent recovery are also subject to the availability of fiscal buffers and the implementation of fiscal and foreign exchange policy frameworks. INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 54 External debt is a key amplifier of the transmission of external shocks. Economies with elevated external debt levels, especially short-term debt, are vulnerable to sudden shifts in investor risk appetite and rollover risks, potentially leading to sudden stops in capital flows and current account reversals. For most LMICs, where external debt tends to be denominated in foreign currencies, economic vulnerabilities can increase when external shocks lead to currency depreciation, causing an increase in debt service burdens and higher inflation. An increase in debt service costs can slow investment growth by decreasing national savings. During periods of tightening global financial conditions, LMICs with high levels

of external debt need to raise interest rates to defend their currencies, causing credit crunches in domestic financial markets and slowing growth. Despite a recent slowdown in international integration, LMICs have become more exposed to external shocks, while also accumulating external debt. In LMICs, although the pace of trade integration has slowed, trade openness, measured as the sum of exports and imports as a share of GDP, increased to about 48 percent in 2025, up from about 44 percent in the mid-2010s (figure 2.3). 2. DEBT DyNAmIcs: POLIcy ImPLIcATIONs 55 2015–19 and 2020–25. Financial openness, represented by the sum of foreign assets and liabilities as a share of GDP, remained nearly unchanged from the mid-2010s through 2024. International financial integration has slowed since the pandemic in 2020, but that slowdown has been driven primarily by major economies; financial openness increased in almost 70 percent of LMICs between 2015–19 and 2020–24. In addition, as presented in chapter 1, external debt stocks in LMICs rose to $9.4 trillion by the end of 2025, an increase of $3.5 trillion since 2015. The nature of external shocks also affects the different degrees of shock transmission to LMICs. For example, global supply shocks, including shortages

of energy, food, and other commodities—and rapid increases in their prices, which tend to be caused by wars and conflicts as well as extreme weatherrelated events—have a larger impact on commodity importers. The outbreak of a conflict involving major commodity producers can halt their exports, and the impact can be exacerbated by logistical disruptions such as port or shipping lane closures. Particularly in food-producing economies, disasters associated with extreme weather, including storms and droughts potentially caused by El Niño, can decrease global food production and disrupt global trade. In addition, abrupt shifts in trade policies, including the imposition of tariffs or export bans, can restrict access to key commodities. In contrast, commodity

exporters tend to be affected more by adverse global demand shocks, including slowdowns in global activity triggered by major systemic events such as financial crises and pandemic-driven lockdowns, and the resulting plunges in commodity prices. In commodity-importing LMICs, external shocks can be transmitted through multiple channels. Higher global energy and food prices, along with disruptions to shipping and global value chains, raise production and transportation costs. The resulting rise in domestic inflation in these economies drives up the cost of living, with disproportionate effects on poorer economies and households, where food accounts for a larger share of consumption. The purchasing power of consumers declines as real incomes

fall, resulting in reduced spending. In addition, higher prices of commodities and other imported materials increase overall import costs, worsening terms of trade and current account balances. Financial conditions can tighten because of hikes in interest rates to combat increased inflation, raising borrowing costs. Pressures of currency depreciation rise, increasing the costs of servicing debt denominated in foreign currencies. Fiscal positions deteriorate, with increasing spending pressures, including fuel and food subsidies, and slower activity can lower revenue collection.

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 56 Inflation in commodity-importing LMICs has increased following a major energy supply shock in 2026. The conflict in the Middle East involving major energy producers, which began at the end of February 2026, has caused a surge in headline inflation in these countries, to 3.6 percent in June 2026, from the preconflict level of 2.6 percent (figure 2.4). Among market participants, inflation expectations for 2026 have also risen, from 2.7 percent according to preconflict February surveys to 3.4 percent in July. Excluding China, which has been relatively insulated from the shock, partly because of its large petroleum reserves, inflation in commodity-importing LMICs increased from 7.0 percent

to 8.3 percent between January and June, with higher inflation expectations for 2026. Energy prices have increased, as well, by 1.1 percentage points between January and June 2026 (excluding China). To ease price pressures, several central banks have raised interest rates. In addition, several commodityimporting LMICs have introduced subsidies in response to higher fuel prices (World Bank 2026b). Among commodity-importing

LMICs with flexible or adjustable exchange rate regimes, currencies depreciated by about 1.7 percent between January and July 2026 (figure 2.5), on average. In contrast, currencies in commodity-exporting LMICs with flexible regimes appreciated by an average of 2.5 percent over the same period. Currency pressures have made imports more expensive in commodity importers and worsened trade balances. Across commodity-importing LMICs with flexible or adjustable currency regimes, merchandise import values, in US dollar terms, increased by an average 23 percent between February and June 2026 compared with the same months of 2025. Excluding China, the rate of increase was 21 percent, on average. As import values increased faster than those of exports,

merchandise trade deficits—without China—expanded in the first half of 2026. Between February and June 2026, merchandise trade deficits averaged almost $20 billion higher than in the same months of the previous year.

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 58 Global demand shocks affect commodity-exporting LMICs directly and indirectly. Collapses in global commodity prices directly reduce export earnings and profits in the commodity-related sector, reducing domestic demand and activity. Revenue declines cause deterioration of fiscal positions and the debt service mechanism, while also leading to worsening terms of trade and current account balances. With reduced debt repayment capacity, sovereign risk premiums increase, raising debt refinancing costs, eroding investor confidence, and potentially triggering sudden capital outflows. Financial conditions are tightened, with lower credit availability and a weakened banking sector, along with a rise in nonperforming

loans. Declines in foreign exchange earnings also lead to currency depreciation, which increases inflationary pressure and living costs. The impact of external shocks tends to be larger and more persistent in fragile economies and low-income countries (LICs). In both LICs and economies in fragile, conflict, and violence-affected environments or with institutional fragility, financial markets tend to be shallower than in other LMICs, making them more exposed to external shocks. They tend to rely on narrower economic bases, in terms of exports and revenue sources, and are therefore more affected by sudden shifts in external conditions. With a weak institutional framework and limited access to financing, these economies tend to implement procyclical

fiscal tightening during economic downturns. Increases in commodity prices and supply shortages translate into substantial losses in economic welfare and income, reflecting persistently low personal savings and acute food insecurity. International reserves and credible monetary policies can help cushion the adverse impact of external shocks in LMICs. The accumulation of foreign exchange reserves can defend against sharp currency depreciation and can be used to pay for imports of commodities and other essential products. LMICs have increased their foreign exchange reserves over the past decade, reaching more than $6 trillion at the end of June 2026. Excluding China, foreign exchange increased to $2.6 trillion in June. However, the pace of foreign exchange accumulation has

slowed since March 2026, particularly in commodity-importing LMICs, mainly because of the conflict in the Middle East (figure 2.6). Facing a rise in import costs driven by currency depreciation, some of these economies have been forced to draw on their reserves. This trend has been exacerbated by outflows of foreign currency, mainly driven by rising global risk aversion. In addition, credible monetary policy frameworks act as critical policy buffers against external shocks in LMICs. They help anchor long-term inflation expectations and reduce the transmission of global shocks, such as commodity price changes and financial market volatility, to domestic inflation. Preconditions for the effectiveness of the frameworks include greater independence for central banks and transparent
communication of monetary policy.

2. DEBT DyNAmIcs: POLIcy ImPLIcATIONs 59 Robust fiscal policy frameworks can also act as strong policy buffers against external shocks. Fiscal rules help manage revenue volatility and excess spending during booms; stabilization funds, especially in commodity-exporting LMICs, can mitigate the procyclicality of fiscal policy by saving revenues during booms and deploying them when commodity prices and revenues collapse. Since 2000, many commodity-exporting LMICs have adopted such frameworks (figure 2.7). However, successful implementation requires strong institutions, including transparency and technical capacity (Vasishtha 2026). Policy priorities differ across LMICs, depending on the strength of institutional capacity and

fiscal space. Economies with weaker capacity need to strengthen tax revenue mobilization and improve fiscal transparency. Debt Sustainability and Fiscal Pressures External shocks have compounded preexisting fiscal pressures and increased debt vulnerabilities in LMICs. These countries require substantial investment to raise productivity, create jobs, and advance broader development objectives.

Financing these needs depends on mobilizing domestic resources, attracting domestic and foreign private capital, and, where necessary, borrowing through public channels. In this context, part of the increase in public debt reflects efforts to finance infrastructure, human capital, and other investments that can support long-term growth. However, slower global growth, policy uncertainty, trade fragmentation, geopolitical tensions, and commodity-price volatility have affected both the availability and cost of financing. In many countries, shocks that initially generated temporary financing needs have contributed to persistently higher debt stocks, debt service burdens, and rollover requirements. The Impact of Higher Debt on Fiscal Space and Financing Pressures

The accumulation of public debt has been accompanied by a substantial increase in debt service burdens in LMICs over the past 25 years. The median total debt service in countries eligible for International Development Association (IDA) assistance increased from about 15 percent of government revenues (excluding grants) in 2000 to over 40 percent in 2025. During the same period,

2. DEBT DyNAmIcs: POLIcy ImPLIcATIONs 61 the composition of IDA countries’ debt burden shifted markedly toward domestic debt; whereas average external debt service underwent a U-shaped trajectory to end up at over 17 percent of revenues by 2025, the average domestic debt service-to-revenues ratio more than trebled, reaching almost 30 percent by 2025 (figure 2.8). The increase in the domestic debt service burden was especially pronounced after 2012, reducing the resources available for public investment and other policy priorities, and increasing the need to refinance maturing obligations. As discussed in box 2.1, proactive and structured engagement with investors and creditors can reduce information asymmetries and help lower the uncertainty of premium embedded in borrowing costs.

These developments have contributed to a sustained increase in gross financing needs (GFNs) in IDA countries. Higher debt service burdens have important implications for fiscal space and refinancing needs. A larger share of government revenues must be allocated to interest payments, leaving fewer resources available for public investment and other policy priorities. INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 62 refinance maturing obligations contributes to elevated GFNs, even when fiscal deficits are narrowing. GFNs in IDA countries averaged about 6 percent of GDP during 2015–19, before increasing to roughly 10 percent during 2020–22 as pandemic-related primary deficits widened and debt service obligations increased. Subsequent shocks, including the commodity price and inflation surge following the Russian Federation’s invasion of Ukraine, and the sharp global monetary tightening that began in 2022, further contributed to elevated financing needs. GFNs subsequently moderated but remained well above their prepandemic average, at approximately 8.2 percent of GDP in 2024, before rising to 8.7 percent in 2025.

Box 2.1 The World Bank Group’s Sovereign Investor Relations Guidance Note Sovereign credit rating actions remained in flux throughout 2025. For instance, in the first half of 2025, Fitch recorded eight sovereign upgrades against four downgrades among emerging markets—a net positive trend—but revised its sector outlook for Asia-Pacific, Eastern Europe, and Sub-Saharan Africa to “deteriorating” from “neutral,” citing trade uncertainty and tightening fiscal space. Moody’s downgraded Bolivia and Botswana, while upgrading Costa Rica. This mixed picture illustrates that sovereign creditworthiness is increasingly differentiated and that the gap between countries that gain and lose market confidence is often shaped not only by fundamentals but also by how effectively governments engage with

investors and creditors. Against this backdrop, the World Bank Group has published “Sovereign Investor Relations: A Guide for Debt Managers” (Proite and Y avuz 2026), a practical handbook designed to help debt managers in low- and middle-income countries build and professionalize their investor relations functions. The guide argues that countries must move from passive disclosure to active, structured engagement that reduces information asymmetries to lower the “uncertainty premium” embedded in their borrowing costs. The guidance note covers the full spectrum of sovereign investor relations, from strategy formulation to institutional setup as well as practical tools for implementation. The guide is scalable and designed for countries

at varying stages of market development, from frontier markets taking their first steps in external borrowing to frequent issuers seeking to deepen and diversify their investor bases. The latest developments in 2026 also reinforce the core message of the guidance note—that is, in a world of differentiated sovereign credit outcomes, proactive investor relations are not a luxury but a strategic necessity. Countries that engage creditors early, communicate policy intent clearly, and manage reputational risk systematically are better positioned to preserve market access, reduce financing costs, and navigate periods of stress.

2. DEBT DyNAmIcs: POLIcy ImPLIcATIONs 63 The persistence of high GFNs, despite narrower primary deficits, underscores the role of accumulated debt and higher debt service costs. Notwithstanding notable fiscal consolidation, with primary deficits in 2023–24 narrowing to approximately half their 2021–22 levels, average GFNs stabilized at about 8 percent of GDP, 2 percentage points above their prepandemic average, before increasing further in 2025. Consistent with this pattern, the distribution of debt-stabilization gaps across countries has changed little over the past 15 years (figure 2.9). These gaps, denoted as ΔDSPD, are calculated as the difference between the actual primary deficit and the debt-stabilizing primary deficit,

indicating the primary deficit or surplus that would keep the debt-to-GDP ratio unchanged, given the country’s existing debt, borrowing costs, and GDP growth.2 This calculation suggests that the continued elevation of GFNs is not primarily the result of a renewed widening of primary deficits. Rather, it reflects the debt stock accumulated following successive shocks, higher interest costs, the rollover of maturing obligations, and, in some cases, balance of payments financing needs. INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 64 Debt distress risks have eased from the deterioration observed over the past decade, particularly following the COVID-19 shock, but they remain elevated. As informed by the World Bank–International Monetary Fund Debt Sustainability Framework for Low-Income Countries (LIC-DSF), the number of IDA LIC-DSF countries with unsustainable external public debt or rated as being in debt distress remains limited (at end-December 2025): out of 68 IDA LIC-DSF countries, only 11 are in debt distress or have unsustainable public debt. The share of IDA LIC-DSF countries assessed as being at high risk of external debt distress declined from a peak of 46 percent in 2021 to 35 percent in 2025. Most emerging markets remain

at low or moderate risk of overall sovereign stress,3 although vulnerabilities remain uneven, and debt levels are generally above prepandemic levels. Despite these improvements, IDA LIC-DSF countries have generally moved from high to moderate risk rather than returning to their preshock levels. Between 2019 and 2025, there were a total of 37 changes in external risk (figure 2.10). Of these changes, 22 were downgraded to higher risk of external debt distress, most of which took place after the COVID-19 shock. More recently, upgrades have reflected improved macro-fiscal conditions and, in a few cases, the completion of debt restructuring. The LIC-DSF framework underpinning these assessments has undergone a comprehensive review by the World Bank

Group and the International Monetary Fund, with that review approved by their respective Executive Boards in September 2026. The revised framework is expected to be finalized in 2027; box 2.2 summarizes its key features. DEBT DyNAmIcs: POLIcy ImPLIcATIONs 65 Box 2.2 Strengthening the Debt Sustainability Framework for Low-Income Countries The 2026 review of the Debt Sustainability Framework for Low-Income Countries by the International Monetary Fund and World Bank Group updates how the organizations assess sovereign debt risk and sustainability amid rising domestic borrowing, diversified creditor bases, and growing liquidity pressures. The revisions aim to strengthen early warning capacity and policy relevance while preserving the framework’s role in guiding borrowing and lending decisions. Key reforms include the following: • A revamped risk architecture distinguishing more clearly between external debt stress, overall public debt stress, and unsustainability

• The introduction of new models for the risk of overall public debt stress and public debt unsustainability, together with an updated model for the risk of external public debt stress • New dedicated modules to support the structured application of judgment, including – A domestic debt module to assess solv ency, liquidity risk, and macrofinancial linkages (including the sovereign–bank–central bank nexus); and – A long-term module t o evaluate implications of policy and investment decisions (including climate adaptation, infrastructure, and human capital) over longer horizons • New emphasis on data quality via the new debt data confidence flag, clearer guidance on the debt perimeter, and incentives to close reporting gaps

• Introduction of additional granularity to risk ratings to differentiate among countries at high risk of debt distress. The review was launched in 2024 with public consultations and stakeholder inputs gathered through 2026. The new framework is expected to become operational in the second half of 2027 , allowing time to finalize the revised operational guidance and undertake extensive capacity building for users of the framework. Source: World Bank 2026c. The Impact of Debt Composition on Liquidity and Domestic Financial Sector Risks The increase in financing needs has been accompanied by greater reliance on domestic debt. Domestic borrowing has provided an important source of financing when access to external markets is limited or costly. However, it
has also increased rollover risks and strengthened the links between sovereign finances and domestic financial sector stability.

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 66 Domestic creditors in both IDA and International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) countries have elevated their exposure to the sovereign over the past 20 years. This move mirrors their respective governments’ growing reliance on domestic financing. However, domestic banks in IDA countries have consistently held a greater share of their balance sheets in sovereign assets than banks in IBRD countries have (figure 2.11). This higher exposure reflects less developed and less diversified private sectors in many IDA countries, as well as fewer investment options as compared to IBRD markets. Domestic banks may therefore have few alternatives to government securities, particularly during

periods of financial stress. In IDA countries, the increase in sovereign exposure goes beyond the domestic banking sector to include the central bank and the domestic nonbanking sector (figure 2.12). Consequently, domestic debt amortization dominates GFNs for LICs, signaling mounting liquidity pressures even where sovereign solvency appears contained. These pressures reflect the short average maturity of domestic debt in most LICs and the attendant rollover burden, whereby a growing share of gross financing serves merely to refinance maturing domestic obligations. point to intensifying liquidity pressures even where solvency indicators may appear contained, reinforcing the case for monitoring rollover and liquidity risks alongside conventional debt stock metrics. Fiscal Policy and Debt Management Higher debt and borrowing costs are absorbing fiscal resources, increasing refinancing risks, and potentially crowding out investment. Weak debt management, limited transparency, foreign currency exposure, and contingent liabilities can amplify these pressures. The result is a reinforcing financing constraint: higher debt service costs reduce fiscal space and limit productive public investment; insufficient public investment weakens the conditions for attracting long-term private capital; and greater reliance on foreign currency

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 68 borrowing increases exposure to exchange rate and refinancing shocks. At the same time, high debt limits countries’ ability to borrow to close financing gaps. Countries are therefore left increasingly exposed to shocks, with minimal fiscal and financial buffers. Sound fiscal and debt policies are central to preparing for, responding to, and recovering from external shocks. Fiscal buffers and debt sustainability determine the extent to which countries can absorb shocks and support recovery. Countries that entered shock episodes with adequate fiscal buffers, manageable debt levels, and a track record of countercyclical policies consistently limited longterm output losses. By contrast, high debt and procyclical spending amplified

the economic damage.4 The interaction of limited fiscal buffers, elevated debt vulnerabilities, and weak policy execution points to three interconnected priorities: revenue mobilization and maintaining sound debt management, adopting countercyclical fiscal strategies, and investing in fiscal institutions. Mobilizing revenue and managing debt. Revenue mobilization is not simply a matter of raising tax rates. Effective mobilization requires a holistic approach that strengthens the policy, administrative, and legal foundations of the tax system in tandem (Benitez et al. 2023). Without this broader institutional underpinning, additional revenue efforts risk being partial, inequitable, or unsustainable, undermining the fiscal resilience they are intended to build.

Effective debt management requires not only controlling the overall level of debt but also managing its composition and risk profile, including maturity, currency, interest rate, refinancing, and creditor risks. Sound debt management acts as a key shock absorber during times of crisis. Poor borrowing choices made during periods of stress can worsen liquidity and solvency risks, particularly when governments turn to short-term solutions that are less transparent or less market based, such as private placements or collateralized borrowing. These instruments may provide immediate financing, but they can also increase rollover risks, reduce transparency, constrain future policy choices, and expose public assets or future revenues to claims. Governments should therefore design, implement, and

communicate contingent borrowing plans before crises occur. Conducting fiscal policy over the economic cycle. Economies that ran procyclical spending policies and persistent deficits over time faced economically larger and longer-lasting output losses from external shocks, whereas those that maintained countercyclical spending and ran primary surpluses, on average, experienced little to no losses. Dependence on commodities for exports and fiscal revenues makes commodityexporting LMICs particularly exposed to swings in commodity prices.

2. DEBT DyNAmIcs: POLIcy ImPLIcATIONs 69 Box 2.3 External Shocks and Fiscal Consolidation Fiscal consolidation following a major external shock is particularly difficult and less likely to preserve growth. For example, consolidation episodes preceded by terms-of-trade shocks were significantly less successful in maintaining per capita growth rates near preconsolidation rates than episodes that were not preceded by such a shock (figure B2.3.1). This result reflects not only policy choices but also the persistent economic damage caused by the shock and the need for governments to support vulnerable households and economic activity before adjustment can begin. Consolidation is often delayed even after fiscal balances become unsustainable,

which carries compounding costs. Where the primary deficit was significantly larger than what would stabilize debt, countries tended to wait three to four years before embarking on meaningful fiscal consolidation (figure B2.3.2; Di Lorenzo and Lacey 2024). Political and social constraints are particularly binding in the aftermath of a shock, but delay can compound the eventual costs. Where large sustainability gaps (that is, the primary deficit was significantly larger than what would stabilize debt) persisted for four years or more, the median debt ratio increased by 17 percentage points of gross domestic product. Growth also weakened: during periods of sustained fiscal unsustainability, average real gross domestic product per capita growth fell to the 32nd percentile of each country’s

own historical distribution. For countries facing high borrowing costs and limited market access, these findings underscore the value of early, credible, and growth-conscious corrective action. During commodity price booms and the resulting rise in fiscal revenues, governments in those economies tend to increase spending. Without primary surpluses, those economies tend to have fewer fiscal resources to support activity and protect vulnerable populations when external shocks hit. Increased spending and debt accumulation during booms may also lead to a loss of market confidence during commodity price busts, requiring a large fiscal adjustment or contributing to debt distress (refer to box 2.3 for more details on external shocks and fiscal consolidation). The implication

is clear: fiscal strategies that save windfalls during economic upturns, such as commodity booms, and deploy those savings during downturns allow governments to respond effectively when shocks arrive. (Box continues on next page)

2. DEBT DyNAmIcs: POLIcy ImPLIcATIONs 71 Establishing credible fiscal institutions and fiscal buffers. When a shock hits, the fiscal impact can be immediate and large, as spending needed to protect vulnerable communities rises while revenues fall. Governments can prepare for this tendency by establishing contingency reserves within the annual budget, natural disaster funds with clear rules governing their use and size calibrated to historical experience, and state-contingent debt instruments and other insurance mechanisms that transfer a portion of disaster risk to third parties (Polacek 2018). Well-designed fiscal rules can reinforce these buffers while allowing temporary, transparent flexibility during severe shocks.

These instruments should be integrated into broader fiscal risk and debtmanagement frameworks. Contingent liabilities, including guarantees to stateowned enterprises, public-private partnerships, financial sector support, and disaster-related obligations, should be identified, monitored, and disclosed. Medium-term expenditure frameworks offer one powerful mechanism for translating these commitments into practice, aligning spending with strategic priorities and ensuring the planning horizon needed to address future shocks before they arrive (World Bank 2012). Food Import Exposure, External Debt Burdens, and Healthy Diet Affordability Food imports are an important channel through which external shocks can affect food and nutrition security. They are particularly relevant as countries face

an uncertain external environment, with geopolitical tensions, weather-related shocks, trade disruptions, and volatility in energy and fertilizer markets posing continued risks to global food markets and prices (FAO 2026; World Bank 2026a). Such shocks may be especially difficult to absorb in economies with high external debt burdens. In countries that rely more heavily on imported food, such shocks can translate into higher domestic food prices, with potentially important implications for household purchasing power, welfare, and diet quality, given the substantial share of food in household consumption, especially in lower-income countries (FAO and World Bank 2018). Previous analysis in International Debt Report 2025 showed that higher external

debt burdens were associated with higher levels of unaffordability of healthy diets across countries (World Bank 2025). This section extends that analysis by examining food import exposure as one important source of vulnerability to external shocks, including the importance of food in merchandise imports, reliance on imported supply across food groups, and the diversification of import sources. It also examines associations between external debt burdens and changes

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 72 in healthy diet unaffordability over time, a broader outcome that reflects both food costs and people’s economic resources. Food Import Shares in Poorer Economies Across the sample, which consists predominantly of LMICs, the share of food in merchandise imports generally declines as income per capita rises (figure 2.13, panel a). By contrast, economies with larger external debt burdens relative to exports also tend to have higher food import shares (figure 2.13, panel b).5 Both relationships matter for an economy’s capacity to manage food import exposure. Lower-income economies may have less room to absorb increases in import costs, and a high debt-to-exports ratio indicates that external debt is

large relative to export earnings. During external shocks, higher import costs can therefore coincide with weaker economic and external buffers; export earnings may also decline, further increasing pressure on foreign exchange resources and raising the debt-to-exports ratio, even without an increase in the debt stock. Import Reliance and Debt Burdens Across Food Groups Aggregate food import shares do not show how strongly the domestic supply of individual food groups depends on international markets. Net import reliance— net imports as a share of domestic supply quantity—varies substantially across the six food groups making up the Healthy Diet Basket (Bai, Herforth et al. 2025; Herforth et al. 2025). Among net importing economies, median reliance is highest

for oils and fats, at 63.6 percent, followed by starchy staples, at 36.9 percent, and legumes, nuts, and seeds, at 34.1 percent. Median reliance is lower for animalsource foods, at 28.0 percent, and for vegetables and fruits, at 17.4 percent and 13.4 percent, respectively. To identify economies where high reliance on food imports and elevated external debt burdens overlap, figure 2.13 applies two reference thresholds. For many economies, high import reliance coincides with elevated external debt burdens. Figure 2.14 highlights economies where external debt stocks are at least 150 percent of exports, as a reference point based on the threshold applied under the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) Initiative,6 and where net

imports account for at least 30 percent of domestic supply in a given food group. The figure intends to identify the coexistence of these two sources of vulnerability, rather than to assess whether higher external debt is associated with greater reliance on food imports. This overlap is most common for oils and fats: 34 economies—about 42 percent of net importers in the group—meet both thresholds. The corresponding shares are about 28 percent for legumes, nuts, and seeds; 27 percent for starchy staples; 23 percent for animal-source foods; 16 percent for vegetables; and 15 percent for fruits.

Another is how concentrated imports are across source economies. An economy that sources a food group from a broader range of suppliers may have more options to adjust when trade with a particular exporter is disrupted than one that depends on only

a few sources. Import source diversity is measured using the Shannon Diversity Index,7 which captures both the number of source economies and how evenly imports are distributed across them; higher values indicate greater diversification. Higher-income economies generally source food imports from a broader and more evenly distributed set of suppliers (Bai, Kaushik et al. 2025). In the sample used for this analysis, upper-middle-income economies have higher median import source diversity than low- and lower-middle-income economies in five of the six food groups,

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 76 with the largest differences for fruits (2.12 versus 1.65) and vegetables (1.99 versus 1.64). Median diversity is similar for starchy staples (1.83 versus 1.88). Animalsource food imports are relatively diversified in both groups, with median Shannon indexes of 2.69 and 2.49, respectively. Analysis for this report reveals that diversity of import sources is also associated with external debt burdens. Higher debt relative to exports is significantly associated with lower import source diversity for starchy staples and, notably, for animal-source foods, fruits, and vegetables—nutritionally important components of a healthy diet that together account for a large share of its

cost (figure 2.15). By contrast, higher debt burdens are associated with greater import source diversity for oils and fats, and for legumes, nuts, and seeds. 2. DEBT DyNAmIcs: POLIcy ImPLIcATIONs 79 Among economies covered by this analysis, healthy diet unaffordability remains particularly high in LICs. The population-weighted prevalence of people unable to afford a healthy diet fell only marginally, from 77.4 percent in 2017 to 76.9 percent in 2025, and increased by 4.0 percentage points during 2019–21. Between 2017 and 2025, unaffordability declined from 58.5 to 45.2 percent in lower-middle-income economies and from 34.2 to 23.2 percent in upper-middleincome economies. During 2017–19, the relationship between changes in healthy diet unaffordability and external debt burdens was weak and not statistically significant. The association became substantially stronger and statistically significant during

2019–21 and remained similarly strong and significant during 2021–23. In these periods, economies with higher debt stocks relative to export earnings tended to experience larger increases, or smaller declines, in healthy diet unaffordability. A doubling of the debt-to-exports ratio was associated with a more adverse change in unaffordability of approximately 1.6–1.8 percentage points. During 2023–25, the relationship weakened again and was no longer statistically significant. As revealed in this section, food import vulnerability reflects both reliance on imported supply and the concentration of import sources, and these dimensions can coincide with high external debt burdens. The period analysis adds an outcome perspective, showing that higher debt burdens are more strongly

associated with nutrition security challenges during major external shocks, as reflected in changes in healthy diet unaffordability. This pattern is consistent with the earlier framing of debt acting as an amplifier of vulnerability, and it highlights the importance of considering food import exposure and external debt together when assessing a country’s nutrition resilience to future external shocks.
